key_finding: A field-experiment nudge that shrouds the minimum-payment autopay option cuts minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but does not reduce credit card debt, and actually raises missed payments by discouraging autopay enrollment among liquidity-constrained cardholders.
methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with 6-month follow-up; JEL-coded econometric analysis of payment behavior.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's worry: a choice-architecture change can shift nominal enrollment/behavior metrics while leaving the real outcome (debt/savings) unchanged or worse, which is exactly the 'vanity enrollment number' risk for the round-up feature.
limitations: credit-card debt repayment context, not a savings product
no direct test of a savings round-up mechanism
liquidity constraints specific to indebted cardholders may not generalize to savers
relevance_reason: Consumer self-directed financial nudge study showing enrollment/behavior change without matching real-outcome improvement, directly bearing on whether defaults would be a vanity metric here.

key_finding: Narrative overview of DC plan design summarizing how automatic enrollment, default investments, framing, and newer features affect participation, contribution rates, and engagement, including potential negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: abstract-only narrative synthesis of the retirement plan design literature.
why_it_matters: Gives a synthesized backdrop on default effects and disengagement risk across the literature we are drawing analogies from, useful context though not itself new evidence for the round-up design.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan context throughout
narrative overview, not a systematic review with effect sizes
no discussion of consumer/self-directed liquid savings settings
relevance_reason: Broad synthesis of the default-effects literature that frames the analogy the brief warns against relying on uncritically.

key_finding: Default enrollment lifts short-term participation but induces long-run passivity (low contribution rates, no active account management, churn), so participation alone is insufficient evidence of welfare improvement; proposes auto-escalation, re-enrollment reminders and financial education as mitigations.
methodology: abstract-only narrative/policy discussion synthesizing prior empirical findings.
why_it_matters: Names concrete mitigation levers (auto-escalation, periodic re-enrollment prompts) that could be built into the round-up feature if an opt-out design is chosen, directly informing the disengagement-mitigation part of the design.
limitations: employer retirement plan framing throughout
narrative synthesis, no new empirical effect sizes
mitigations proposed are pension-specific (auto-escalation of contribution rate, not multiplier)
relevance_reason: Articulates the 'passive trap' concern and mitigation strategies directly relevant to the disengagement risk the support team raised.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when defaults do or do not produce lasting ('downstream') behavior change, keyed to time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
methodology: Theoretical synthesis and taxonomy-building drawing on the existing default-effects literature; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a framework for predicting and measuring whether the round-up default will produce genuine lasting engagement versus a superficial enrollment bump, directly shaping what to track at 6-12 months.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical, no new empirical effect sizes
general consumer behavior framework, not specific to financial savings products
relevance_reason: Directly targets the brief's central question of whether default effects on enrollment persist into real downstream behavior, with a framework for measurement.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization for low-income beneficiaries, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive even when the default option causes substantial welfare losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a US public health insurance program.
why_it_matters: Shows that default-driven passivity can persist even when it actively harms the defaulted population, cautioning against assuming a round-up default is costless for less-engaged users; also flags that active-choice variation may be driven by transitory attention shocks rather than stable engagement.
limitations: public health insurance for low-income/elderly beneficiaries, not a discretionary consumer financial product
no discussion of contribution-level anchoring
US Medicare-specific institutional context
relevance_reason: Strong evidence that default enrollment can persist and harm passive users, directly bearing on the distributional/manipulation-risk question even though outside the financial-product domain.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of auto-escalation defaults are followed at the first escalation date, declining further later.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover, withdrawal upon separation, and auto-escalation opt-out, abstract-only for further detail.
why_it_matters: The clearest statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift is real at signup and much smaller later, and preset escalation is not durably followed — a direct caution against treating opt-out enrollment counts as the success metric.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
abstract gives limited detail on mechanisms behind opt-out of escalation
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving durably, which the brief explicitly asked us to look for.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees into the public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most enrollees actively opted out; the default effect is stronger when incentives are higher and when individuals lack knowledge of their enrollment status.
methodology: Natural experiment using nationwide policy rollout, linked administrative and survey data.
why_it_matters: Provides a recent, large, quantified default effect size and shows it is moderated by incentive salience and awareness — directly useful as a benchmark for how big an opt-out lift we might see, and a warning that most gains may reverse via opt-out.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension via employer-like payroll system, not a standalone consumer app
no data on persistence of the minority who stay enrolled beyond initial opt-out window
no data on amounts saved, only participation
relevance_reason: Recent, well-quantified opt-out default effect size in a savings-adjacent government program, useful as an anchor even though not a consumer fintech setting.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's gains in participation and contributions, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, with only modest average savings increases at the longer horizon though inequality in savings is reduced; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of roughly $250.
methodology: Data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel; life-cycle consumption-savings model estimation.
why_it_matters: Direct medium-run evidence that the initial enrollment lift from an opt-out design shrinks over time, supporting caution before treating headline enrollment numbers as a durable success metric for the round-up feature.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans in the US and UK, not consumer liquid savings
model-based extrapolation of lifetime effects rather than direct field data at longer horizons
relevance_reason: Quantifies attenuation of default enrollment effects at a medium-run horizon (36 months), directly speaking to the persistence question the brief raises.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift investment risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but lower ratings of advice quality compared to no default, especially when the targeted default is refused; framing of the default question (how much to invest vs. how much to leave safe) also shifts the amount allocated to the risky option.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, in a wealth-management/investment-advice context.
why_it_matters: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern reputational risk of defaults in financial products, and shows preset framing anchors the invested/allocated amount — bearing on both the entry-mechanism and preset-level decisions.
limitations: investment risk-taking with a wealth manager, not a round-up savings multiplier specifically
experimental/survey setting rather than a live product deployment
relevance_reason: EU consumer-financial experiment on default framing effects on both behavior and perceived manipulation, hitting nearly every sub-criterion the brief cares about.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at all three studied firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and the conservative default fund, with half still at the default rate and fund after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms over several years.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that defaults anchor not just enrollment but the contribution level and investment choice itself — the classic evidence the preset-multiplier decision has to reckon with.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan context, pre-dating current fintech/regulatory environment
no liquid/self-directed consumer savings analogue
no discussion of active choice as an alternative
relevance_reason: The classic, heavily-cited foundational study establishing that default levels anchor participant contribution choices, which the later literature in this scan argues with.

key_finding: In a structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost ('friction complementarity'), and structural parameters stay stable when the default menu changes, implying defaults channel behavior through frictions rather than reshaping preferences.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million tipping transactions, validated against an independent stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Offers a transferable friction-decomposition framework (deviation cost vs. opt-out/effort cost) for understanding why a preset round-up multiplier might anchor user choice, useful for interpreting anchoring data once the feature ships.
limitations: domain is taxi tipping, not financial savings
consumer stakes and decision frequency differ substantially from a savings-level choice
relevance_reason: Contributes a general structural framework for default adherence mechanisms directly applicable to interpreting whether the preset multiplier anchors user choice.

key_finding: An opt-in payroll-deduction short-term savings program across five UK firms saw very low take-up (no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account), but among those who did enroll, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of a payroll-deduction liquid savings account rollout at five UK firms, tracked over 12 months.
why_it_matters: The closest available analog to a round-up-style liquid savings product: it shows opt-in alone yields minimal enrollment even for a well-liked, persistent product, directly informing the entry-mechanism decision.
limitations: employer payroll intermediary rather than a standalone consumer banking app
UK employer-workplace context, not the app sign-up flow we are designing
no test of opt-out or active-choice alternatives
relevance_reason: Directly studies opt-in enrollment into a liquid short-term savings product structurally similar to round-up savings, showing extremely low take-up despite strong persistence among adopters.

key_finding: A general characterization shows that when designer and chooser preferences align, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal for default design, with extensions to externalities, Pigouvian fees, and normative ambiguity.
methodology: Theoretical/analytical derivation of asymptotic optima with numerical simulations verifying approximation accuracy; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides a normative economic framework for choosing which enrollment default or preset level minimizes costly opt-outs while respecting heterogeneous user preferences, useful for reasoning about which multiplier to preset.
limitations: purely theoretical, no empirical validation in any consumer savings context
abstract gives no domain-specific numbers or population
relevance_reason: Offers a general economic theory of optimal default design applicable to choosing an enrollment or level default that minimizes friction while respecting preference heterogeneity.

key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to classify when EU-regulated defaults and other choice-architecture practices constitute manipulative 'dark patterns.'
methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy-building; abstract-only, no empirical data.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU legal framework for judging whether an opt-out or pre-checked default in the round-up feature would read as a dark pattern, directly informing the reputational-risk assessment of the entry-design decision.
limitations: Legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence of behavioral effects
No effect sizes or outcome data
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern/manipulation risk criterion central to the entry-design decision.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, only 25% of employees had opted out at 12 months, versus roughly 50% opt-out under lower defaults, and low-income employees were disproportionately anchored at the suboptimal default rate.
methodology: Observational analysis of administrative payroll/plan data from an employer retirement plan with a high default contribution rate.
why_it_matters: Shows persistence of defaults at 12 months and quantifies how a high preset rate can anchor low-income savers at a suboptimal level, a caution for which multiplier to pre-select.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer app
No engagement/withdrawal data beyond opt-out status
relevance_reason: Closest quantitative evidence on default persistence and anchoring at high preset levels, despite being in the employer-plan setting the brief flags as only an analogy.

key_finding: Abstract not available (truncated to 'Trant'); title indicates field experiments on automating short-term UK payroll savings.
methodology: abstract-only; large-scale U.K. field experiments implied by title, no further detail available.
why_it_matters: Potentially relevant short-term (non-retirement) savings-automation evidence from the same research group behind other automatic-enrollment studies, but the abstract gives nothing usable.
limitations: Abstract is corrupted/unavailable so no verifiable findings
Likely payroll (employer-mediated) context rather than a consumer app
relevance_reason: Title suggests short-term automated savings experiments relevant to round-up savings, but no extractable content.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts reduced unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though enrolled consumers still captured less than half of available savings.
methodology: Large-scale field experiments at major UK banks testing automatic enrollment into SMS alerts.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that a bank can auto-enroll consumers into a low-friction financial feature with measurable real-world benefit, but also that auto-enrollment alone leaves much potential benefit unrealized, cautioning against treating enrollment numbers as the full picture.
limitations: Alerts, not a savings-contribution product, so amount-saved dynamics may differ
No multi-year retention or withdrawal data reported
relevance_reason: Same setting as the brief (UK consumer bank, self-directed customers) and directly tests automatic enrollment's real effect size and gap versus potential benefit.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment increased savings by roughly £32-38/month but was partially offset by increases in unsecured debt (~£7/month) and higher mortgage balances (~£118) over 41 months, with credit scores rising modestly.
methodology: Large-scale randomized roll-out of automatic enrollment pensions across ~160,000 UK employers, natural experiment design.
why_it_matters: Warns that a 'successful' enrollment default can be substantially offset by behavioral responses elsewhere, meaning enrollment or nominal pot growth may overstate the true net benefit of an opt-out design.
limitations: Employer-mediated pension enrollment, not a self-directed consumer app
Offsetting-debt mechanism may not exist for liquid round-up savings
relevance_reason: Directly challenges the premise that default-driven savings increases translate into net financial benefit, a core question in the brief.

key_finding: Removing an auto-enrollment default and adding a minor extra sign-up step ('ordeal') for health insurance reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying the removal of an auto-enrollment policy in a health insurance market, with a selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Shows that adding friction, as active choice or opt-in effectively does, can produce large, inequitable enrollment declines concentrated among disadvantaged groups, a direct warning for the distributional risk of choosing opt-in or active choice over opt-out.
limitations: Health insurance selection market, not a consumer savings product
Adverse-selection dynamics specific to insurance may not apply to savings
relevance_reason: Provides a large, quantified equity cost of adding sign-up friction, directly bearing on the distributional criterion for choosing among entry designs.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest effects on smaller, less-experienced donors who likely did not intend recurring commitments.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences natural experiment across U.S. political campaign websites' donation checkout pages.
why_it_matters: Direct real-world evidence that a pre-checked recurring-transaction default, structurally identical to auto-enrolling users into an ongoing round-up commitment, drives unintended enrollment and refund/complaint-like behavior concentrated on the least-experienced users, exactly the support team's disengagement/complaint concern.
limitations: Political donations, not a savings product, though the recurring-default mechanism directly transfers
No 6+ month retention data beyond refund requests
relevance_reason: Demonstrates the mechanism the brief calls a dark default, a pre-checked recurring financial commitment, causing complaint-like behavior disproportionately among vulnerable users; the recurring-transaction default is an explicit method transfer to the round-up default question.

key_finding: In a lab search experiment, defaults raised the reservation utility of searchers via a reference effect, and those who rejected the default were more likely to find better options via self-selection, both effects empirically confirmed.
methodology: Controlled behavioral economics experiment on search behavior with a default option.
why_it_matters: Offers a general mechanism for why defaults can improve outcomes even for people who reject them, but doesn't address enrollment, persistence, or financial products directly.
limitations: Generic lab search task, not a financial or enrollment decision
No consumer financial application or effect on money saved
relevance_reason: Tangential behavioral-economics evidence on default psychology, weakly connected to the enrollment/anchoring questions.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual from 15 months after rollout, showing active choice can durably shift users away from a preset default.
methodology: Difference-in-differences natural experiment around EU DMA-mandated choice-screen rollout across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Large-scale EU-regulatory-era evidence that mandated active choice can substantially and durably overcome an incumbent default, the most directly on-point test of whether active choice captures most of the benefit of a default, in the exact regulatory environment the round-up feature will launch into (the method transfer: a forced-choice screen mandated to counteract a persistent platform default).
limitations: Mobile browser choice, not a financial savings decision
Platform-specific rollout differences complicate generalization
relevance_reason: The most directly on-point evidence in this shortlist for the active-choice-vs-default comparison, in the EU regulatory context named by the brief.

key_finding: A usability study of nine opt-out interface designs for Global Privacy Control found that 'generalizable' active-choice schemes reduced disruption (98% not-disrupted for the best scheme, a 40-point improvement) with only a slight cost to opt-out utility, and 83% of participants understood the mechanism.
methodology: Browser-extension usability study with 410 participants comparing multiple non-default opt-out interface designs.
why_it_matters: Offers concrete interface-design principles for making an active-choice, non-default enrollment screen low-friction and legally robust, directly useful if the team pursues the active-choice entry design.
limitations: Privacy opt-out context (CCPA), not financial savings enrollment
No enrollment or savings-amount outcomes measured
relevance_reason: Provides transferable UI-design guidance for building a usable active-choice screen, relevant to the active-choice entry option.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-up in all cases, but improved actual exam completion only for a single high-endorsement exam and only among students previously responsive to university communication; non-responsive students showed increased sign-up but no gain in actual completion.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up defaults to opt-out in two university study programs.
why_it_matters: Empirically demonstrates the exact failure mode the support team predicts: an opt-out default can inflate nominal enrollment while doing nothing for the effortful behavior among less-responsive users, directly bearing on whether opt-out enrollees actually engage with the savings pot.
limitations: University exam context, not a financial product
Heterogeneity defined by past responsiveness to university communication, which may not map onto banking-app users
relevance_reason: Directly tests whether opt-out defaults translate into effortful engagement versus nominal sign-up, the central persistence/depth question in the brief.

key_finding: After target-date funds became the default investment in retirement plans post-2006, younger and older workers' equity allocations diverged in line with the TDF glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel analysis of millions of U.S. retirement investors, 2006-2018, around the Pension Protection Act policy change.
why_it_matters: Suggests a changed default can strongly anchor a downstream choice while leaving a separate contribution-level decision largely unmoved, a caution that a preset round-up multiplier might shift secondary choices without changing overall saving behavior.
limitations: Employer retirement plan investment defaults, not consumer savings-rate defaults
Allocation-anchoring findings may not transfer to a simple multiplier choice
relevance_reason: Weak but relevant data point that a preset default did not change contribution/participation levels, bearing on whether presets truly change amount saved.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, all tested behavioral nudges, including default options, significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings in China, with default-option and positive-narrative nudges producing the largest backfire and effects varying by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working assumption that defaults reliably raise enrollment/contribution, showing defaults can backfire in a self-directed savings context with highly heterogeneous effects by demographic group, exactly the caution the brief asks for.
limitations: Chinese cultural/institutional context, not EU
Online survey RCT measuring stated willingness, not real enrollment or 6-12 month persistence in an actual product
relevance_reason: The explicit contradicting evidence the brief asked for: a controlled experiment where default nudges reduced rather than increased savings intent.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people generally approved of financial nudges (positive on approval, benefit, ethics) except on manipulation, with stronger approval for System 2-targeting interventions framed around saving rather than spending.
methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment presenting 36 hypothetical financial-intervention vignettes to a representative Australian sample (n=2,100), factorially varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting.
why_it_matters: Shows which framing and mechanism choices make a financial default read as helpful rather than manipulative, directly informing how the entry flow and disclosure copy for the round-up feature should be designed to avoid a dark-pattern perception.
limitations: hypothetical vignette approval ratings, not revealed enrolment or savings behaviour
Australian sample, not the EU regulatory context
no measure of actual retention or amount saved
relevance_reason: Directly measures when a financial nudge/default is perceived as manipulative versus acceptable, the exact reputational-risk question the brief raises.

key_finding: Offering conditional cash transfer beneficiaries a choice of receiving transfers via bank account instead of cash had no significant average effect on savings, but raised balances specifically among those with previously nonpositive balances.
methodology: Randomized offer of an alternative delivery mechanism to CCT beneficiaries, comparing downstream savings, assets and trust outcomes; abstract-only detail.
why_it_matters: Suggests that account-based savings mechanisms mainly help those starting from zero rather than lifting savings broadly, a caution for how enrolment gains from our round-up feature should be interpreted.
limitations: developing-country cash-transfer population, not EU banking-app users
does not compare opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment architectures
measures account balances, not habitual round-up saving behaviour
relevance_reason: Weak analogy on consumer choice of savings mechanism and heterogeneous effects by prior savings level.

key_finding: Describes program design variants of a universal automatic IRA that pairs retirement contributions with a liquid emergency-savings component, noting that liquid-fund availability can differ across designs even when contribution amounts are identical.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to be a policy-design comparison rather than an experiment.
why_it_matters: Touches on pairing a liquid, accessible pot with automatic enrolment, similar in spirit to a round-up savings pot, but the abstract is too thin to extract an actionable finding.
limitations: abstract is a truncated fragment with almost no substantive detail
IRA/retirement-account context rather than a discretionary consumer app
no reported effect sizes on enrolment, persistence, or amount saved
relevance_reason: Nominally on-topic for pairing liquid savings with automatic enrolment but too sparse to be actionable.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrolment dramatically raised participation, and a large share of newly auto-enrolled employees stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation, treating the default as implicit advice.
methodology: Before/after administrative data analysis of 401(k) elections at one large U.S. corporation following a switch to automatic enrolment.
why_it_matters: The original demonstration that defaults raise both headline enrolment and anchor the chosen contribution level, the exact anchoring risk the brief raises for the pre-set round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer product
no employer-trust-free analogue
predates modern fintech and EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: Foundational study establishing the default-enrolment effect and default anchoring on contribution level, the two mechanisms the brief's decisions turn on.

key_finding: Title indicates a comparison of savings behaviours between automatic and voluntary enrolment in a defined-contribution retirement plan; no abstract is available.
methodology: abstract-only
why_it_matters: Could add another data point on auto- vs voluntary-enrolment savings behaviour, but with no abstract there is nothing concrete to act on.
limitations: no abstract provided, content and effect sizes unknown
employer/DC retirement plan setting, not a consumer app
relevance_reason: Title matches the enrolment-design question but lack of content prevents assessment of actual relevance.

key_finding: Limited trust in financial institutions and non-national/minority status were significantly associated with both under-saving and early withdrawal from retirement accounts following a pension-freedom reform in Estonia.
methodology: Analysis of three nationally representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) surrounding an early-withdrawal pension reform.
why_it_matters: Warns that passively enrolling low-trust or minority users into a savings feature could disproportionately leave exactly those users withdrawing early or under-saving, direct evidence for the distributional-harm concern the brief raises.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme with a policy-driven withdrawal option, not a discretionary consumer savings app
Estonian population, not EU-wide banking-app users
correlational survey design, not causal
relevance_reason: Directly evidences the heterogeneity/distributional-harm and persistence-of-engagement questions the brief asks about, despite the pension rather than app setting.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent survey experiment across G7 countries, prompting people to reflect on being automatically enrolled in a booster-vaccine appointment reduced stated vaccination intentions and reduced approval of the default policy.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment manipulating reflection on a hypothetical default-enrolment policy across G7 countries.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults are costlessly effective: making a default salient can trigger backlash, relevant to how transparently we should disclose an opt-out design under EU norms.
limitations: health/vaccination policy setting, not a financial product
measures stated intentions and approval, not actual enrolment or savings behaviour
hypothetical scenario rather than a live product
relevance_reason: The clearest evidence in the shortlist that surfacing a default can backfire, contradicting the 'defaults always help without cost' assumption.

key_finding: Using 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study data, automatic enrolment and employer matching were both associated with higher likelihood of retirement-plan participation among Millennials, while their absence was linked to non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis with regression controls for debt, income, risk tolerance and assets.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the standard employer-plan default effect on enrolment but adds nothing on persistence, amount saved, anchoring, or active choice, so it does not move either open decision.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan reliant on employer trust/matching, a mechanism the brief says does not transfer
correlational, not causal
no consumer fintech or liquid-savings outcome measured
relevance_reason: Another confirmatory employer-401k auto-enrolment study, included for completeness but largely duplicative of settled findings.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic employer contributions substantially raised wealth accumulation while tax subsidies requiring active choice mostly shifted assets across accounts (raising total saving by only about 1 cent per dollar of subsidy); about 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' driven by automatic contributions rather than incentives.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel analysis of the Danish population's retirement and taxable savings accounts, comparing responses to active-choice subsidies versus passive automatic contribution changes.
why_it_matters: The strongest available evidence that a default/automatic mechanism changes real saved amounts, not just nominal enrolment, while an active-choice mechanism mostly reshuffles assets for a minority of sophisticated actors — directly bearing on whether an opt-out round-up default would raise actual savings versus just headline enrolment.
limitations: Danish retirement/tax-advantaged accounts partly administered through employers, not a discretionary consumer banking app
concerns long-horizon wealth accumulation, not weeks-to-months round-up engagement
no direct active-choice-vs-opt-out enrolment comparison
relevance_reason: Answers the brief's central question about amount saved versus nominal enrolment with large-scale causal evidence and rich heterogeneity, despite the retirement-account setting.

key_finding: Field experiments show that 'active choice' (forcing a decision, no default) and a novel 'enhanced active choice' design (highlighting the losses of the non-preferred option) can motivate behavior change as an alternative to opt-out defaults, especially where automatic enrolment is infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against control conditions, building explicitly on the active-choice enrolment literature (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, Metrick 2009).
why_it_matters: Introduces and field-tests the exact 'active choice' entry mechanism the brief is weighing, plus an 'enhanced active choice' variant that could capture much of a default's enrolment lift without the disengagement cost of opt-out.
limitations: evidence base is medication adherence, not financial products
no measurement of contribution-level anchoring or long-run amount saved
the loss-framing nudge in enhanced active choice itself risks a manipulative/dark-pattern read
relevance_reason: The key paper directly proposing and testing the active-choice design alternative named in the brief's entry decision, with an explicit note that its logic was built for savings/opt-out contexts.

key_finding: A field-wide review of behavioral household finance summarizing empirical regularities in saving, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, and cataloguing intervention types (education, peer effects, product design, disclosure, choice architecture, and price/quantity levers) used to shape household financial behavior.
methodology: Narrative literature review / NBER chapter synthesizing behavioral household-finance research; abstract gives no specific effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Provides the broad synthesis-level map of which choice-architecture levers work in individual financial behavior, reminding the team that product design and disclosure are viable alternatives or complements to a straight default.
limitations: broad survey chapter, not focused specifically on enrolment defaults
abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes
spans both employer-mediated and self-directed settings without separating the two
relevance_reason: Serves as the shortlist's synthesis/review anchor on choice architecture in individual financial behavior.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of new participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years, so the participation gain and anchoring-driven under-saving roughly offset on average, though non-participation among the lowest savers still fell sharply.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing 401(k) participation, contribution rates and fund choices before/after automatic enrolment.
why_it_matters: The clearest existing demonstration that a default can raise headline enrolment while anchoring people at a low pre-set level that offsets much of the savings gain on average, precisely the risk the brief flags for a pre-set round-up multiplier.
limitations: 401(k) employer-plan context reliant on employer trust and payroll deduction, not a discretionary consumer app
predates modern fintech and EU regulatory environment
no measure of subjective engagement, complaints, or dark-pattern perception
relevance_reason: Foundational quantitative evidence for both the persistence question (3-year data) and the anchoring question, central to whether a pre-set default multiplier suppresses the level people would otherwise choose.

key_finding: A randomized field experiment among Afghan government employees found default enrolment in a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% matching incentive), driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of thinking through savings scenarios, and defaulted employees became more likely to actively choose to keep saving after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment varying default enrolment plus follow-up mechanism-testing interventions on salary-linked savings accounts for government employees in Afghanistan.
why_it_matters: Offers a quantified default effect size and rare evidence that a default-driven saving habit persisted into active choice after the intervention ended, speaking directly to the brief's worry that defaulted users disengage rather than internalize the behavior.
limitations: salary-linked account tied to employer/government payroll, not a self-directed consumer banking app
low-income developing-country civil servants, unlike EU app users
no measure of amount saved or withdrawal, only participation and post-study attitudes
relevance_reason: Provides a quantified default effect size plus mechanism and post-intervention persistence evidence, directly bearing on whether enrolment gains are real or merely nominal.

key_finding: A field-experiment reminder nudge cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with the harm concentrated in users with an overdraft history who saw a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, using administrative fee data across credit card and checking accounts.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's concern that a nudge/default which helps on average can systematically harm a vulnerable subgroup, making the case for measuring heterogeneous outcomes (e.g. overdraft-prone or low-balance users) rather than just aggregate enrolment or savings lift before deciding on opt-out enrolment.
limitations: studies payment reminders rather than enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchoring
Brazilian credit/overdraft market context, not EU round-up savings
no explicit 6-12 month persistence tracking of the intervention's effect
relevance_reason: Provides rigorous, consumer-financial-app RCT evidence of exactly the distributional harm-to-a-subgroup risk the brief flags as a reason not to build something that only 'works on average'.
